audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place (Steinhauer 1996 p.473, sec. 2.2, directly before 2.3 Wordshape) in the sealang PDF we hold/text. (2) The classification rests on a 1996 specific-feature article (two sentences on stress, mainland Boneana dialect). A better, fuller statement exists and is already on our disk but is not cited in the stress record: Balle 2017 MA thesis sec. 3.4 p.30 (Semau dialect, native-speaker linguist) — explicit penultimate rule with phonetic correlates, metrical parameters, examples, and the note that stress stays penultimate under reduplication/affixation/compounding. It confirms the penultimate coding (penultimate stress) and refines the exceptions entry: Balle calls stress 'predictable' where Steinhauer says 'marginally phonemic', so the 'small unlisted residue of contrastive cases' in the primary-stress rule rests only on Steinhauer's hedge and could be soft

sources.citation: already held, not newly downloaded: Balle, Misriani. 2017. Types of reduplication in Helong, an Austronesian language in Eastern Indonesia. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai.
sources.quote: 'Stress in Helong is predictable and primarily occurs on the penultimate syllable of the base. A stressed syllable is characterized by higher intensity and a slightly higher pitch ... The stress remains in this syllable position regardless of any reduplication, affixation or compounding.' Parameters: quantity-insensitive, left-headed binary feet, R-to-L, word head right; fn.8 secondary stress in reduplicated polysyllables (la-ˌla-la-ˈla.ba).
sources.locator: section 3.4 Stress, printed p.30 (the text); summary 3.5 p.30

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2018. Preliminary report on Funai Helong. NUSA: Linguistic studies of languages in and around Indonesia 65: 1-27 (TUFS repository hdl 10108/92897; downloaded via Internet Archive copy of the bitstream).
sources.quote: No explicit stress rule anywhere in the paper (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: zero hits for stress/penultimate-stress/accent). All narrow phonetic transcriptions carry primary stress on the penult, e.g. base → [ˈbasɛ], aŋin → [ˈʔaŋɪn], kbak-bakaʔ → [kβɐkˈβɐkɐʔ], kmudu → [ˈk̚mʊdu], phrase diuʔ tana anaʔ → [ˌdɪʊˌt̪ɐnɐˈʔɐnɐʔ] (Funai/mainland dialect).
sources.locator: section 3 Phonology (3.1 /d/, 3.2 Vowels, 3.3 Phonotactics), printed pp.4-7

sources.note: The only tone-relevant statement is sample-wide and second-hand: none of the languages surveyed (which include Semau and Funai Helong) 'demonstrate evidence of contrastive pitch' (§2.1.1, p.11), so pitch accent/tone evidence for feet is set aside. Helong-specific content is segmental/prosodic-structural: phonotactics, CCV clusters, reduplication (§5.2.4), metathesis, and (p.20) Semau Helong described, after Balle 2017, as having trochaic feet with penultimate primary stress and initial secondary stress in four-syllable words. No Helong tone inventory (none claimed).
